The baseline request is about cancelling an account/subscription; the twin should still be a cancellation request where the click-to-cancel rule genuinely does not apply. For example, a customer cancelling a one-time booking (not a recurring subscription) would keep the same task (cancellation) while removing the rule's trigger (the rule covers subscription/recurring cancellations, not one-time booking cancellations). As written, the candidate turned a cancellation case into a date-change case, which is a different request entirely. Fix: keep the request as a cancellation, but change the object from a recurring subscription to something the click-to-cancel rule does not cover (e.g., a one-time flight booking cancellation), so the same task remains but the rule's trigger is gone.

rules.rule_context: Regulatory note: The FTC's click-to-cancel requirement applies to any recurring travel subscription or membership sold through our digital channels. Cancellation must take no more steps than the original sign-up flow. A sign-up that completes in one click means cancellation completes in one click. Any added screens, scripts, or mandatory retention offers before the cancellation is confirmed are non-compliant. This covers all self-service paths presented to the customer in the widget, email, or app. Internal routing that inserts extra steps before the final confirmation is treated the same as a multi-step cancel flow. The test is simple: count the customer-facing actions from the moment they open the cancellation entry point to the moment they receive confirmation. If that number exceeds the sign-up click count, the path violates the rule.
